newsitem.title: USA: GPU porposes phased-in rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: GPU porposes phased-in rate cuts.

text.p: GPU Energy said Tuesday its plan to implement competition and customer choice for its New Jersey electric consumers includes a 10 percent rate reduction, of which 2.1 percent was implemented in April.
The GPU Inc subsidiary has proposed, in a filing with the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, the remaining reduction would be phased in over two years starting October 1, 1998.

GPU Energy said its filing covers the three addressed in the board's Findings and Recommendations for restructuring the New Jersey electric power industry released in April -- Unbundled Rates, Stranded Costs and Restructuring Plan.
GPU Energy said its rate unbundling plan includes the 10 percent rate reduction.

Separate from GPU Energy's proposed reduction, it noted, there will be an additional rate reduction of about 6 percent phased in over the next six years, as a result of tax reform legislation signed into law by Governor Whitman Monday.

Based on computer modeling to simulate the future power market and project electricity prices, GPU Energy's filing estimates stranded costs of its New Jersey subsidiary, Jersey Central Power & Light, at about $1.8 billion, of which $1.6 billion are for non-utility generation contracts.

GPU pointed out it has already reduced non-utility generation contracts by some $3.2 billion in New Jersey alone. It noted the board's Final Report would allow New Jersey electric utilities to fully recover their prudently-incurred stranded costs -- investments and commitments that may not be recoverable in a competitive environment.
Other utilities operating in the state are Atlantic Energy Inc, Public Service Enterprise Group Inc and Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc.

GPU said one method of stranded cost mitigation it supports is securitization, a refinancing mechanism which involves issuing securities known as transition or rate reduction bonds. GPU Energy would use the proceeds from these bonds to retire outstanding securities or reduce stranded costs, if this mechanism is authorized by state legislation.
The bonds would be repaid by a transition charge on all delivery customers and the savings realized in refinancing costs could then be passed on to customers.

"Legislation must be enacted to provide the authority for utilities to recover stranded costs in order for securitization to be an effective method for rate reduction," said Elizabeth Ard, vice president of corporate affairs for New Jersey. "Securitization will save customers money. We need legislation to provide that opportunity."

GPU said it proposes a non-utility generation transition charge to allow for the recovery costs, over the life of federally mandated non-utility generation contracts that are priced over the market value of electricity.

Its filing also proposes a market transition charge over a four-year period which covers above market nuclear and fossil fueled plants and purchases from other utilities. These charges are currently a part of existing rates, GPU noted.
The market transition charge does not include above-market costs associated with the Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station which GPU proposes removing from rates effective September 1, 2000.
It said the investment costs associated with Oyster Creek would be recovered as regulatory assets in the distribution portion of the unbundled rates.
GPU reiterated no final decision has been made on Oyster Creek's future.
GPU said it will act as the backup supplier if deliveries aren't made or an alternative supplier will no longer serve a customer once the market is opened to competition.

Its filing adopts phased in supplier choice as proposed by the board but limits this choice by commercial and industrial customers to those with hourly metering, adding those without this equipment have the same option if they choose to have hourly metering installed.
